analysis.one_liner: Requires large companies to test and report whether their automated decision systems harm consumers.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by 12 Senate Democrats, the bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies above a size threshold that use software to help make life-changing decisions — about jobs, credit, housing, health care, insurance, and more — would have to run ongoing 'impact assessments': testing the system's accuracy, privacy risks, and whether its results differ by race, sex, age, disability, or income. They would file summary reports with the Federal Trade Commission, which would publish trends and a searchable public registry of who uses automated decisions and how consumers can contest one. The FTC would get a new Bureau of Technology and 75 additional staff to review and enforce these rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose lives are increasingly shaped by algorithms — job applicants screened out by hiring software, borrowers denied credit, renters refused housing, patients steered in health care, and people flagged by fraud or content systems. The bill gives them testing, documentation, a public registry, and a documented route to appeal or opt out of these decisions.

how_it_helps.text: Requires covered companies to test automated decision systems for accuracy, privacy risk, and differential performance by race, sex, age, disability, income, veteran status, and other characteristics before and after deployment.
Requires companies to attempt to eliminate or mitigate any likely material negative impact found, and to document — with reasons — any harms they leave unmitigated.
Requires an FTC public repository showing which companies use automated decision systems for which critical decisions, and how a consumer can contest, correct, appeal, or opt out of a decision.

Covers decisions with legal or material effects on employment, credit, housing, health care, education, utilities, family planning, and legal services, and lets state attorneys general sue to enforce the law on residents' behalf.
Creates an FTC Bureau of Technology with at least 50 technologist hires plus 25 additional enforcement staff, so the agency can actually review the systems rather than take companies at their word.

analysis.who_pays: Large companies that develop or deploy automated decision systems — tech firms, lenders, insurers, employers, and landlords above the bill's size thresholds — bear the cost of ongoing testing, documentation, stakeholder consultation, and annual reporting to the FTC. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through higher prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large tech firms and algorithm-using companies

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes substantial compliance costs — ongoing testing, documentation, and stakeholder consultation — on companies above roughly $50 million in receipts or handling data on over a million consumers, and some portion of those costs is likely to reach consumers through prices.

The most detailed assessments stay confidential: companies must file only summary reports with the FTC, and the bill expressly does not require disclosing the full impact assessment to the Commission or the public, limiting outside scrutiny.

The bill mandates testing and reporting but does not ban any particular practice outright; a company can document a harm, state its rationale, and continue using the system, so its real effect depends on FTC enforcement.
The thresholds exempt smaller companies, so many landlords, employers, and services using off-the-shelf automated tools would not be covered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real compliance cost for large companies in exchange for documented testing, disclosure, and a public record of systems that decide jobs, credit, housing, and health care. The design has limits — the full assessments stay private and nothing is banned outright — but the public registry and state-enforcement provision give consumers and researchers genuine visibility they do not have today.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never held a hearing or vote, so the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden introduced the Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2023 on September 21, 2023, joined by 11 Democratic senators including Booker, Warren, Casey, Baldwin, Merkley, Whitehouse, Schatz, Hirono, Heinrich, Peters, and Luján.

The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; the action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
All 11 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that use automated systems to make decisions about jobs, credit, housing, and health care keep operating without testing or disclosure requirements, and the FTC gains no new authority to examine them. Consumers gain nothing from a bill that never advanced.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2023 and recruited 11 Democratic cosponsors.

for.role: Cosponsors (Booker, Heinrich, Peters, Casey, Luján, Baldwin, Merkley, Whitehouse, Schatz, Hirono, Warren)

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never took it up — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the action history through the end of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration at any point in the 15 months it was pending.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; no vote ever occurred, so the partisan split on the merits was never tested on the floor.

industries.note: The bill would require them to test their automated decision systems, document harms, consult outside stakeholders, and report annually to the FTC, with a public registry exposing where their systems decide housing, credit, and employment. Their interest in avoiding testing and disclosure runs against consumers who want to know how they are being judged.

industries.industry: Lenders, insurers, employers, and landlords using automated decisions
industries.note: Their screening and pricing algorithms fall squarely within the bill's 'critical decisions', forcing performance testing by race, sex, age, disability, and income — exactly the analysis that can expose discriminatory outcomes. Consumers on the receiving end of those decisions gain the counterpart protections.
The bill would create demand for third-party audits, impact-assessment services, and privacy-enhancing technology, a new market whose growth depends on the same testing consumers want.
